question: Measurement in physics means
opt_a: writing only the name of a quantity without a value
opt_b: replacing all quantities by the same unit
opt_c: guessing the size of an object from its appearance
opt_d: comparison with a chosen standard unit
explanation: Measurement is the process of finding how many times a chosen standard unit is contained in a physical quantity. For example, saying a table is 2 m long means its length has been compared with the standard unit 1 m . A guess may be useful in daily life, but it is not a reliable measurement in physics. A measurement is also incomplete if it gives only a quantity name without a numerical value and unit. The standard unit makes the result understandable and repeatable for different observers.

question: The statement “a measured quantity is expressed as ______” is completed by
explanation: A measured physical quantity needs both a numerical value and a unit. In symbolic form, it may be written as Q = n u , where Q is the physical quantity, n is the numerical value, and u is the unit. For instance, in 5 m , the number is 5 and the unit is m . The number alone does not tell whether the measurement is in m , cm , or another unit. The unit gives the scale with which the quantity has been compared.

question: In the statement “the length of a table is 1.2 m ”, the physical quantity being measured is
explanation: The physical quantity is the measurable property of the object, so here it is the length of the table. The number 1.2 is only the numerical value obtained after measurement. The symbol m is the unit used for comparing the length. The object itself is not the measured quantity; a property of the object is being measured. Keeping quantity, number, and unit separate prevents early confusion in measurement language.

question: A road distance is written once as 2 km and once as 2000 m . The item that remains the same in both records is the
explanation: The same road distance is being described in both records. The numerical value changes from 2 to 2000 because km and m are different-sized units. The physical distance does not become larger just because the number becomes larger. A smaller unit gives a larger numerical value for the same quantity. This is why a measurement must always be read as number plus unit, not as number alone.

question: A measuring tape gives the width of a notebook as 18 cm . In this record, the unit is
explanation: In 18 cm , the symbol cm is the unit used to express the measured width. The number 18 tells how many such units are counted. The word width names the physical quantity, not the unit. The notebook is the object whose property is being measured. A measurement record becomes meaningful only when the numerical value is attached to a definite unit.

question: Standard units are needed mainly because they
opt_a: make every numerical value equal to 1
opt_b: allow measurements to be compared reliably
explanation: A standard unit provides a common reference for measurement. If different people use different personal units, their results may not be comparable. For example, measuring a desk in handspans can give different numbers for different people. A standard such as m gives a fixed scale independent of the observer. Reliable comparison is one of the main reasons physics uses agreed units.

question: Two people measure the same stick using their own handspans and obtain different numbers. The best explanation is that
opt_b: every measurement must have the same number
opt_c: handspan is not a reproducible standard unit
opt_d: the stick changed length during measurement
explanation: A handspan varies from person to person, so it is not a fixed standard unit. The stick may have the same physical length, but the numerical value depends on the size of the unit used. A longer handspan gives a smaller number of handspans for the same stick. This does not show that length is impossible to measure. It shows why physics prefers well-defined standards instead of body-based units.

question: The pair that shows a physical quantity followed by a suitable unit is
explanation: Volume measures the space occupied by a body, and m 3 is a suitable unit for volume. The unit m is used for length, not mass. The unit s is used for time, not length. The unit kg is used for mass, not time. A quantity-unit pair must match the physical property being measured.

question: A floor area is reported as 12 m 2 . This record shows that
opt_a: area and length are the same quantity
opt_c: the number 12 alone is the complete measurement
opt_d: area is expressed using a square unit
explanation: Area measures the extent of a surface, so its unit is built from length multiplied by length. In SI-based notation, this gives a unit such as m 2 . Length itself is measured in m , so area and length are related but not the same quantity. The number 12 becomes meaningful only with the unit m 2 . The power 2 in the unit signals that a surface, not a line length, is being measured.

question: A bottle label gives volume 750 cm 3 , a package gives mass 0.50 kg , and a stopwatch gives time 30 s . These records all show that measured quantities are written with
explanation: Each record combines a numerical value with a unit. The volume has 750 with cm 3 , the mass has 0.50 with kg , and the time has 30 with s . The quantities are different, but the structure of the measurement record is the same. The unit tells the scale used in the comparison. Without the unit, the numerical value would not identify the size of the physical quantity clearly.

question: A physical quantity is best described as a property that can be
explanation: A physical quantity is a measurable property such as length, mass, time, area, volume, or speed. Measurement gives a numerical value, and the unit tells the standard used for comparison. A property that cannot be measured or compared with a unit does not function as a physical quantity in this sense. Naming a property is not enough to make a measurement. The measurable nature of the property is what connects physical quantities to experiments and observations.

question: The group containing only fundamental physical quantities from the usual mechanics starting set is
explanation: Length, mass, and time are fundamental quantities in the usual beginning treatment of mechanics. They are not defined in terms of other mechanical quantities. Speed, area, density, force, volume, energy, acceleration, pressure, and work are derived quantities because their definitions use other quantities. For example, speed uses length and time. The distinction is about how a quantity is defined, not about whether it is useful.

question: Speed is treated as a derived quantity because it is obtained from
opt_b: luminous intensity and amount of substance
explanation: Speed describes how much distance or length is covered per unit time. Its basic relation is v = distance time . Since it depends on length and time, it is not a fundamental quantity in the mechanics starting set. A derived quantity is formed by combining fundamental quantities through a definition or formula. The unit m s − 1 also shows that speed is built from m and s .

question: Match the introductory symbols with the quantities they usually represent. Symbol Quantity P. l 1. Time Q. m 2. Speed R. t 3. Length S. v 4. Mass The matching that fits the usual notation is
explanation: The symbol l commonly represents length in elementary measurement contexts. The symbol m is commonly used for mass, while t represents time. The symbol v is often used for speed or velocity depending on context. These symbols are not units; they stand for physical quantities. Confusing a quantity symbol with a unit symbol can lead to wrong interpretation of formulas and measurement records.

question: Consider the following statements.
explanation: Statement I is valid because length, mass, and time are taken as fundamental quantities in the usual mechanics foundation. Statement II is also valid because density is defined using mass and volume, as in ρ = m V . A quantity formed from other quantities by definition is called a derived quantity. Statement III reverses the classification: time is not treated as derived from speed and length in the basic system. Speed is the derived quantity because it uses length and time.

question: A record gives density using the relation ρ = m V . This relation shows that density is
opt_a: a derived quantity formed from mass and volume
opt_b: a unit without a physical quantity
opt_c: a fundamental quantity independent of other quantities
opt_d: only a numerical value with no unit
explanation: The relation ρ = m V defines density as mass per unit volume. Since density is obtained by combining mass and volume, it is a derived quantity. Mass is a basic quantity in the usual mechanics set, while volume is itself related to length cubed. Density is not merely a number because it must be reported with a unit such as kg m − 3 . The formula shows both the meaning of the quantity and the reason for its classification.

question: A unit is best understood as
opt_a: the name of the instrument used in measurement
opt_b: the numerical value written before a quantity
opt_c: any word written after a number
explanation: A unit is a fixed standard chosen for comparison with a physical quantity. When a length is measured in m , the metre is the standard unit used to express that length. The numerical value tells how many units are contained in the quantity, but it is not itself the unit. An instrument may help in measurement, but the instrument name is not the measurement unit. A unit must have a defined size so that measurements made at different places can be compared reliably.

question: Complete the statement: A physical quantity Q expressed as Q = n u has n as the ______ and u as the ______.
explanation: In the expression Q = n u , Q represents the physical quantity being measured. The symbol n gives the numerical value, meaning how many times the chosen unit is contained in the quantity. The symbol u represents the unit or standard used for comparison. For example, in Q = 5 m , the number 5 is n and m is u . This form also shows why changing the unit changes the number even when the actual physical quantity remains unchanged.

question: A length is first written as 3 m and then as 300 cm . The change from 3 to 300 happens because
opt_b: m is a smaller unit than cm
opt_c: cm is a smaller unit than m
explanation: The physical length is the same in both records. Since 1 m = 100 cm , the unit cm is smaller than the unit m . A smaller unit must be counted more times to cover the same length, so the numerical value becomes larger. The number therefore changes inversely with the size of the unit. Reading only the number without the unit would make 3 and 300 look inconsistent even though both represent the same length.

question: A laboratory note says, “The mass of the object is 0.25 kg .” If the same mass is expressed in g , the numerical value becomes
explanation: Given quantity: Mass = 0.25 kg . Required: The numerical value when the unit is changed from kg to g . Unit relation: 1 kg = 1000 g . Conversion: 0.25 kg = 0.25 × 1000 g Calculation: 0.25 × 1000 = 250 So the same mass is 250 g . The unit g is smaller than kg , so the numerical value must become larger. Final answer: The numerical value is 250 when the mass is written as 250 g .

question: A measurement record uses \(Q=n u\). If the unit \(u\) is replaced by a unit \(u'\) that is twice as large, the new numerical value for the same \(Q\) becomes
explanation:
\( \textbf{Starting relation:} \) The same physical quantity is written as \(Q=n u\).
\( \textbf{Changed unit:} \) The new unit is twice the old unit, so \(u'=2u\).
\( \textbf{Same quantity condition:} \) The physical quantity does not change, so \(Q=n'u'\).
Substitute \(u'=2u\):
\[
Q=n'(2u)
\]
But \(Q=n u\), so
\[
n u=2n'u
\]
Cancel the common unit \(u\):
\[
n=2n'
\]
Therefore,
\[
n'=\frac{n}{2}
\]
A larger unit is counted fewer times in the same physical quantity.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The new numerical value is \(\frac{n}{2}\).

question: A distance of \(5000\,\text{m}\) is rewritten as \(5\,\text{km}\). This is an example of
opt_b: changing only the unit of the same distance
opt_c: removing the unit from the measurement
opt_d: changing both the quantity and its dimension
explanation: The distance \(5000\,\text{m}\) and \(5\,\text{km}\) represent the same physical length. The change occurs because \(1\,\text{km}=1000\,\text{m}\). When a larger unit is used, fewer units are needed to express the same distance. The dimension of the quantity remains length in both cases. A unit conversion changes the numerical value and unit together, not the actual physical quantity.

question: The expression \(7.5\,\text{s}\) is meaningful as a measurement because
opt_b: a value with a defined time unit
opt_d: any symbol after a number makes a standard unit
explanation: The measurement \(7.5\,\text{s}\) gives both a numerical value and a unit. The unit \(\text{s}\) is a defined standard for measuring time. A decimal number alone does not identify the physical quantity being measured. A random symbol after a number would not be enough unless it represents an accepted unit. The record is meaningful because it tells both the amount and the standard of comparison.

question: A claim says, “The value \(120\) is always larger than \(2\), so \(120\,\text{cm}\) is longer than \(2\,\text{m}\).” The flaw in the claim is that it compares
opt_b: a derived quantity with a fundamental quantity
opt_d: only numerical values without converting units
explanation: The claim compares \(120\) and \(2\) without considering that the units are different. Since \(1\,\text{m}=100\,\text{cm}\), \(2\,\text{m}=200\,\text{cm}\). Therefore \(120\,\text{cm}\) is shorter than \(2\,\text{m}\), even though \(120\) is numerically greater than \(2\). Numerical values can be compared directly only when the units are the same or properly converted. In measurement, the unit is part of the meaning of the value.

question: The International System of Units is commonly abbreviated as
explanation: The International System of Units is abbreviated as \(\text{SI}\), from the French name of the system. It provides internationally accepted base units and derived units for scientific measurement. Using one agreed system reduces confusion when measurements are shared across laboratories, books, and countries. Other systems such as \(\text{CGS}\), \(\text{FPS}\), or \(\text{MKS}\) have been used in physics, but \(\text{SI}\) is the standard modern system. The abbreviation \(\text{SI}\) refers to the system, not to a single physical quantity.

question: The SI base unit of thermodynamic temperature is
explanation: Thermodynamic temperature is one of the seven SI base quantities. Its SI base unit is kelvin, written with the unit symbol \(\text{K}\). The symbol \(\text{cd}\) is the candela, used for luminous intensity. The symbol \(\text{mol}\) is used for amount of substance, and \(\text{A}\) is used for electric current. The case of \(\text{K}\) matters because unit symbols in SI are written in fixed forms.

question: In a formula sheet, \(m\) is used for mass and \(\text{m}\) is used for metre. The difference between these two symbols is that
opt_a: \(m\) is the SI unit of mass, while \(\text{m}\) is the SI unit of time
opt_b: both are unit symbols with the same meaning
opt_c: \(m\) is usually a quantity symbol, while \(\text{m}\) is a unit symbol
explanation: In physics notation, the italic-style symbol \(m\) commonly represents the quantity mass. The roman unit symbol \(\text{m}\) represents metre, the SI base unit of length. A quantity symbol and a unit symbol can look similar in plain writing, but their meanings are different. The SI base unit of mass is \(\text{kg}\), not \(\text{m}\). Careful notation prevents confusing the mass of an object with the metre used to measure length.

The unit \(\text{mol}\) belongs to amount of substance, not luminous intensity. This distinction matters because both luminous intensity and amount of substance are separate SI base quantities. The repaired row would read luminous intensity — \(\text{cd}\).

question:
Consider the following statements about SI base quantities.
I. Amount of substance has the unit \(\text{mol}\).
II. Luminous intensity has the unit \(\text{cd}\).
III. Electric current has the unit \(\text{K}\).
The valid statements are
explanation: Amount of substance is an SI base quantity and its unit is mole, written as \(\text{mol}\). Luminous intensity is also an SI base quantity and its unit is candela, written as \(\text{cd}\). Electric current has the SI base unit ampere, written as \(\text{A}\), not kelvin. The symbol \(\text{K}\) is reserved for thermodynamic temperature. The seven SI base quantities have distinct unit symbols, so swapping symbols changes the meaning of the record.

question: A measurement note records a temperature as \(300\,\text{K}\) and a current as \(2\,\text{A}\). The unit symbols show that
opt_a: both quantities are measured in the same base unit
opt_b: only temperature is a measurable physical quantity
opt_c: \(\text{K}\) is for current and \(\text{A}\) is for temperature
opt_d: temperature and current are different SI base quantities
explanation: Thermodynamic temperature and electric current are two different SI base quantities. Their SI base units are \(\text{K}\) and \(\text{A}\), respectively. The different unit symbols show that the two records refer to different kinds of measurable properties. The number attached to the unit tells the amount on that unit scale, but the unit identifies the physical nature of the measurement. A unit symbol should not be interchanged just because both quantities are part of the SI system.

question: The unit record that keeps quantity symbol and unit symbol roles separated is
explanation: The record \(t=5\,\text{s}\) uses \(t\) as the quantity symbol for time and \(\text{s}\) as the SI unit symbol for second. This is the usual structure of a measurement statement: quantity equals numerical value times unit. Writing the unit symbol as if it were the measured quantity confuses the role of symbols. The unit \(\text{s}\) is a standard, while \(t\) represents the actual time interval being measured. Clear separation of quantity symbols and unit symbols makes equations and measurement records easier to interpret.

question: A quantity obtained by combining base quantities according to a defining relation is called
explanation: A derived quantity is formed from one or more base quantities through a physical definition or formula. For example, area is obtained from length multiplied by length, and speed is obtained from length divided by time. The name does not mean the quantity is less useful; it only describes how it is built. A base unit such as \(\text{m}\) or \(\text{s}\) belongs to a base quantity, while a derived unit such as \(\text{m s}^{-1}\) belongs to a derived quantity. The classification depends on the defining relation of the quantity.

question: The unit of area is written as \(\text{m}^2\) because area is formed by
explanation: Area measures the extent of a surface, and for a rectangle it is found using length multiplied by breadth. Both length and breadth are measured in \(\text{m}\) in SI. Multiplying the units gives \(\text{m}\times\text{m}=\text{m}^2\). This is why \(\text{m}^2\) is a derived unit, not a new independent base unit. The square on the unit shows that two length factors are involved.

question: The unit that naturally represents volume in SI is
explanation: Volume measures the space occupied by a body in three dimensions. For a cuboid, volume is obtained as length \(\times\) breadth \(\times\) height. If each length is measured in \(\text{m}\), the unit becomes \(\text{m}\times\text{m}\times\text{m}=\text{m}^3\). The unit \(\text{m}^2\) belongs to area, where only two length factors are used. The power \(3\) in \(\text{m}^3\) signals that volume involves three length dimensions.

question: The expression for speed becomes meaningful in SI when the blank is filled as \(v=\frac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}}\), so the unit is ______.
explanation: Speed is distance travelled per unit time. In SI, distance is measured in \(\text{m}\) and time is measured in \(\text{s}\). Dividing distance by time gives the unit \(\frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}}\), which is written as \(\text{m s}^{-1}\). The negative power \(\text{s}^{-1}\) means “per second,” not negative time. The unit \(\text{m s}\) would mean metre-second, which represents multiplication rather than division by time.

question: A car covers \(180\,\text{m}\) in \(12\,\text{s}\). Its average speed in SI unit is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) Distance \(=180\,\text{m}\), time \(=12\,\text{s}\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Average speed.
\( \textbf{Useful relation:} \)
\[
v=\frac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}}
\]
This relation applies because average speed compares total distance covered with total time taken.
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
v=\frac{180\,\text{m}}{12\,\text{s}}
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
\frac{180}{12}=15
\]
So,
\[
v=15\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
The unit \(\text{m s}^{-1}\) appears because distance is divided by time.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The average speed is \(15\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).

question: Acceleration has the SI unit \(\text{m s}^{-2}\) because it describes change in
explanation: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity with time. Velocity has the unit \(\text{m s}^{-1}\), and dividing it by time \(\text{s}\) gives \(\text{m s}^{-2}\). The power \(\text{s}^{-2}\) appears because time is involved once in velocity and once more in the rate of change. Force per unit area gives pressure, not acceleration. Energy per unit time gives power, which has a different derived unit.

question: A velocity changes from \(4\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) to \(16\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) in \(6\,\text{s}\). The acceleration and its unit are
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) Initial velocity \(u=4\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), final velocity \(v=16\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), time \(t=6\,\text{s}\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Acceleration.
\( \textbf{Relation:} \)
\[
a=\frac{v-u}{t}
\]
This relation is used because acceleration is change in velocity per unit time.
\( \textbf{Change in velocity:} \)
\[
v-u=16-4=12\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
a=\frac{12\,\text{m s}^{-1}}{6\,\text{s}}
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
a=2\,\text{m s}^{-2}
\]
The second factor of time in the denominator changes \(\text{m s}^{-1}\) into \(\text{m s}^{-2}\).
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The acceleration is \(2\,\text{m s}^{-2}\).

question: In SI, the unit \(\text{kg m s}^{-2}\) is given the special name
explanation: Force is related to mass and acceleration by \(F=ma\). In SI, mass has unit \(\text{kg}\) and acceleration has unit \(\text{m s}^{-2}\). Therefore the unit of force is \(\text{kg m s}^{-2}\). This derived unit is given the special name newton, written as \(\text{N}\). The special name is convenient, but it still represents a unit built from SI base units.

question: Using \(F=ma\), the SI unit of force is obtained as
explanation:
\( \textbf{Formula used:} \) \(F=ma\).
\( \textbf{Unit of mass:} \) \(m\) as mass is measured in \(\text{kg}\).
\( \textbf{Unit of acceleration:} \) \(a\) is measured in \(\text{m s}^{-2}\).
\( \textbf{Unit substitution:} \)
\[
\text{unit of }F=(\text{kg})(\text{m s}^{-2})
\]
\( \textbf{Simplification:} \)
\[
\text{unit of }F=\text{kg m s}^{-2}
\]
This unit is also called \(\text{N}\).
The option \(\text{kg m}^2\text{s}^{-2}\) belongs to work or energy, not force.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The SI unit of force is \(\text{kg m s}^{-2}\).

question: A force of \(10\,\text{N}\) moves a body through \(3\,\text{m}\) in the direction of force. The work done is expressed in
explanation: Work is measured by multiplying force by displacement in the direction of force. The unit of force is \(\text{N}\), and the unit of displacement is \(\text{m}\). Therefore the unit of work is \(\text{N m}\). This derived unit is given the special name joule, written as \(\text{J}\). The unit \(\text{N s}\) is not the SI unit of work, and \(\text{kg m s}^{-2}\) is only the unit of force before multiplying by displacement.

question: The SI base-unit form of \(1\,\text{J}\) is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Starting unit:} \) \(1\,\text{J}=1\,\text{N m}\).
\( \textbf{Unit of newton:} \)
\[
1\,\text{N}=1\,\text{kg m s}^{-2}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitute into joule:} \)
\[
1\,\text{J}=(1\,\text{kg m s}^{-2})(1\,\text{m})
\]
\( \textbf{Combine length factors:} \)
\[
\text{m}\times\text{m}=\text{m}^2
\]
So,
\[
1\,\text{J}=1\,\text{kg m}^2\text{s}^{-2}
\]
The extra factor of \(\text{m}\) comes from displacement in the work expression.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(1\,\text{J}=1\,\text{kg m}^2\text{s}^{-2}\).

question: Power is work done per unit time. Its SI unit is
explanation: Power measures the rate at which work is done or energy is transferred. Since work has unit \(\text{J}\) and time has unit \(\text{s}\), power has unit \(\frac{\text{J}}{\text{s}}\). This is written as \(\text{J s}^{-1}\), and it is also called watt, written as \(\text{W}\). The unit \(\text{J s}\) would mean joule multiplied by second, not joule per second. The negative power on \(\text{s}\) shows division by time.

question: A machine does \(600\,\text{J}\) of work in \(20\,\text{s}\). The power developed is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) Work done \(W=600\,\text{J}\), time \(t=20\,\text{s}\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Power.
\( \textbf{Useful relation:} \)
\[
P=\frac{W}{t}
\]
Here \(W\) denotes work, while the unit watt is written as \(\text{W}\); the meanings are different.
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
P=\frac{600\,\text{J}}{20\,\text{s}}
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
P=30\,\text{J s}^{-1}
\]
Since \(1\,\text{W}=1\,\text{J s}^{-1}\),
\[
P=30\,\text{W}
\]
The result describes the rate of doing work, not the total work itself.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The power developed is \(30\,\text{W}\).

question: Pressure is force per unit area. Its SI unit in base-unit form is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Definition:} \) Pressure is force divided by area.
\( \textbf{Symbolic relation:} \)
\[
p=\frac{F}{A}
\]
\( \textbf{Unit of force:} \)
\[
\text{N}=\text{kg m s}^{-2}
\]
\( \textbf{Unit of area:} \)
\[
\text{m}^2
\]
\( \textbf{Unit of pressure:} \)
\[
\frac{\text{kg m s}^{-2}}{\text{m}^2}
\]
\( \textbf{Simplification of length powers:} \)
\[
\frac{\text{m}}{\text{m}^2}=\text{m}^{-1}
\]
So the SI base-unit form is \(\text{kg m}^{-1}\text{s}^{-2}\).
This unit is also called pascal, written as \(\text{Pa}\).
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The base-unit form of pressure is \(\text{kg m}^{-1}\text{s}^{-2}\).

A watt is the unit of power, and \(1\,\text{W}=1\,\text{J s}^{-1}\). Pascal is the unit of pressure, but pressure is force per unit area, so \(1\,\text{Pa}=1\,\text{N m}^{-2}\), not \(1\,\text{N m}^{2}\). The sign of the power on \(\text{m}\) distinguishes division by area from multiplication by area.

question: Plane angle in radian measure is defined as the ratio of
explanation: Plane angle in radians is defined by comparing the arc length with the radius of the circle. If an arc of length \(s\) subtends an angle \(\theta\) at the centre of a circle of radius \(r\), then \(\theta=\frac{s}{r}\). Since both \(s\) and \(r\) are lengths, their ratio has no dimension. The radian is still used as a named unit to show that the number represents an angle. This avoids confusing a pure number used for angle with a pure number used for some other ratio.

question: An arc of length \(2.0\,\text{m}\) is cut from a circle of radius \(4.0\,\text{m}\). The angle subtended at the centre is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) Arc length \(s=2.0\,\text{m}\), radius \(r=4.0\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Angle \(\theta\) in radians.
\( \textbf{Relation for radian measure:} \)
\[
\theta=\frac{s}{r}
\]
This relation applies because radian measure compares arc length with the radius of the same circle.
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
\theta=\frac{2.0\,\text{m}}{4.0\,\text{m}}
\]
\( \textbf{Cancellation of units:} \) The unit \(\text{m}\) cancels because both numerator and denominator are lengths.
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
\theta=0.50
\]
The angle is written as \(0.50\,\text{rad}\) to show that the dimensionless number is an angular measure.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The angle subtended is \(0.50\,\text{rad}\).

question: The unit steradian is associated with the measurement of
explanation: Steradian is the unit used for solid angle. A plane angle describes opening in a plane, while a solid angle describes spread in three-dimensional space. Just as radian is related to the ratio of arc length to radius, steradian is related to a ratio involving area and radius squared. The quantity is dimensionless because it is based on a ratio of like dimensional combinations. The unit name helps identify the kind of dimensionless angular measure being discussed.

question:
Assertion: An angle measured in radians is dimensionless.
Reason: In \(\theta=\frac{s}{r}\), both \(s\) and \(r\) have the dimension of length.
opt_a: Assertion is true, but Reason is false
opt_b: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason explains Assertion
opt_c: Assertion is false, but Reason is true
opt_d: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason does not explain Assertion
explanation: The assertion is true because an angle in radians is obtained from a ratio of two lengths. In the relation \(\theta=\frac{s}{r}\), the arc length \(s\) and the radius \(r\) both have dimension \([L]\). Their ratio is therefore \(\frac{[L]}{[L]}=1\), so the angle has no dimension. The reason gives the exact dimensional explanation of the assertion. The radian symbol is still written in many physical expressions to show that the number represents an angular quantity rather than an unrelated pure number.

question: A formula uses an angular displacement written as \(3\,\text{rad}\). The best interpretation of \(\text{rad}\) in this record is that it
opt_a: makes angle have the dimension of time
opt_b: gives angle a separate base dimension
opt_c: changes angular measure into a length
explanation: A radian does not introduce an additional base dimension. It is connected with the ratio \(\frac{s}{r}\), where both \(s\) and \(r\) are lengths. This makes the angle dimensionless in dimensional analysis. However, writing \(\text{rad}\) is useful because it tells the reader that the pure number represents an angle. Without the unit name, \(3\) could be mistaken for an ordinary numerical factor rather than an angular measure.

question: A circular track has radius \(10\,\text{m}\). A marker moves through an angle of \(0.40\,\text{rad}\) at the centre. The arc length covered is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Known values:} \) Radius \(r=10\,\text{m}\), angle \(\theta=0.40\,\text{rad}\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Arc length \(s\).
\( \textbf{Radian relation:} \)
\[
\theta=\frac{s}{r}
\]
Rearranging gives
\[
s=r\theta
\]
This is valid because \(\theta\) is in radians; the radian is treated as dimensionless in the multiplication.
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
s=(10\,\text{m})(0.40)
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
s=4.0\,\text{m}
\]
The result has unit \(\text{m}\) because radius supplies the length dimension.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The arc length covered is \(4.0\,\text{m}\).

question: The prefix \(\text{kilo}\) in SI notation represents the factor
explanation: The prefix \(\text{kilo}\) means \(10^3\), or one thousand times the base unit. Thus \(1\,\text{km}=10^3\,\text{m}\) and \(1\,\text{kg}=10^3\,\text{g}\), although \(\text{kg}\) itself is the SI base unit of mass. Prefixes are attached to units to express very large or very small quantities conveniently. The prefix \(\text{milli}\) means \(10^{-3}\), while \(\text{micro}\) means \(10^{-6}\). Confusing \(\text{kilo}\) with a negative power gives numerical values in the wrong direction.

question: A length of \(6.5\,\text{km}\) is equal to
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given measurement:} \) \(6.5\,\text{km}\).
\( \textbf{Prefix meaning:} \) \(\text{kilo}=10^3\).
So,
\[
1\,\text{km}=10^3\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Conversion:} \)
\[
6.5\,\text{km}=6.5\times10^3\,\text{m}
\]
The metre is smaller than the kilometre, so the numerical value in metres must be larger.
\(6.5\times10^{-3}\,\text{m}\) would incorrectly treat \(\text{kilo}\) as a small-unit prefix.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(6.5\,\text{km}=6.5\times10^3\,\text{m}\).

question: The symbol \(\mu\) used in \(\mu\text{m}\) represents
explanation: The prefix symbol \(\mu\) represents micro, which means \(10^{-6}\). Therefore \(1\,\mu\text{m}=10^{-6}\,\text{m}\). The prefix \(\text{nano}\) represents \(10^{-9}\), and \(\text{milli}\) represents \(10^{-3}\). The symbol \(\mu\) should not be replaced by ordinary \(\text{m}\), because \(\text{m}\) is the unit symbol for metre or the prefix symbol for milli depending on position and context. Prefix symbols are case- and symbol-sensitive, so a small change in writing can change the factor.

question: A wire has diameter \(0.25\,\text{mm}\). Expressed in metres, this diameter is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given value:} \) Diameter \(=0.25\,\text{mm}\).
\( \textbf{Prefix relation:} \) \(\text{milli}=10^{-3}\), so \(1\,\text{mm}=10^{-3}\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Conversion setup:} \)
\[
0.25\,\text{mm}=0.25\times10^{-3}\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Scientific notation adjustment:} \)
\[
0.25=2.5\times10^{-1}
\]
So,
\[
0.25\times10^{-3}=2.5\times10^{-1}\times10^{-3}
\]
\[
=2.5\times10^{-4}
\]
The value becomes a small number in metres because \(\text{mm}\) is much smaller than \(\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(0.25\,\text{mm}=2.5\times10^{-4}\,\text{m}\).

question: A data sheet writes \(4.0\,\text{MW}\) for power. The prefix \(\text{M}\) in this record means
explanation: The prefix symbol \(\text{M}\) represents mega, which means \(10^6\). Therefore \(4.0\,\text{MW}=4.0\times10^6\,\text{W}\). The uppercase symbol \(\text{M}\) must not be confused with lowercase \(\text{m}\), which can mean milli as a prefix or metre as a unit symbol depending on context. SI prefix symbols are case-sensitive. This is why \(\text{MW}\) and \(\text{mW}\) represent powers differing by a factor of \(10^9\).

question: The pair of conversions that is consistent with SI prefixes is
explanation: The prefix \(\text{milli}\) means \(10^{-3}\), so \(1\,\text{mm}=10^{-3}\,\text{m}\). The prefix \(\text{nano}\) means \(10^{-9}\), so \(1\,\text{nm}=10^{-9}\,\text{m}\). Both are smaller than a metre, so their conversion factors must involve negative powers of ten. A positive power would incorrectly make \(\text{mm}\) or \(\text{nm}\) larger than \(\text{m}\). Prefixes are best handled by replacing the prefix with its power of ten before doing any calculation.

question: A measurement is changed from \(3.0\,\text{m}\) to \(\text{mm}\). The new numerical value is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Original measurement:} \) \(3.0\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Relation between units:} \) \(1\,\text{mm}=10^{-3}\,\text{m}\), so \(1\,\text{m}=10^3\,\text{mm}\).
\( \textbf{Conversion:} \)
\[
3.0\,\text{m}=3.0\times10^3\,\text{mm}
\]
The numerical value increases because millimetre is a smaller unit than metre.
Using \(3.0\times10^{-3}\) would mean converting \(\text{mm}\) to \(\text{m}\), not \(\text{m}\) to \(\text{mm}\).
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The new numerical value is \(3.0\times10^3\).

question: A length is \(750\,\mu\text{m}\). Its value in \(\text{mm}\) is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given value:} \) \(750\,\mu\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Prefix meanings:} \) \(1\,\mu\text{m}=10^{-6}\,\text{m}\) and \(1\,\text{mm}=10^{-3}\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Relation between \(\mu\text{m}\) and \(\text{mm}\):} \)
\[
1\,\text{mm}=10^{-3}\,\text{m}=1000\times10^{-6}\,\text{m}=1000\,\mu\text{m}
\]
So,
\[
1000\,\mu\text{m}=1\,\text{mm}
\]
\( \textbf{Conversion:} \)
\[
750\,\mu\text{m}=\frac{750}{1000}\,\text{mm}=0.75\,\text{mm}
\]
The numerical value becomes smaller because \(\text{mm}\) is a larger unit than \(\mu\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(750\,\mu\text{m}=0.75\,\text{mm}\).

question: A compact memory line for common prefixes is \(\text{kilo}=10^3\), \(\text{milli}=10^{-3}\), and \(\text{micro}=10^{-6}\). The missing entry in \(\text{giga}=\,\_\_\_\_\) is
explanation: The prefix \(\text{giga}\) represents \(10^9\). It is used for very large quantities, such as \(1\,\text{GHz}=10^9\,\text{Hz}\). The prefix \(\text{mega}\) represents \(10^6\), which is smaller than giga by a factor of \(10^3\). The prefix \(\text{nano}\) represents \(10^{-9}\), which is the opposite side of the power-of-ten scale. The sign of the exponent tells whether the prefix makes the unit larger or smaller than the base unit.

question:

RecordPrefix symbolPower of ten

The entry that needs correction is
explanation: The prefix symbol \(\text{k}\) stands for kilo, so \(10^3\) is correct. The prefix symbol \(\text{m}\) stands for milli, so \(10^{-3}\) is correct when it is used as a prefix. The symbol \(\mu\) stands for micro, so \(10^{-6}\) is also correct. The prefix symbol \(\text{M}\) stands for mega, which means \(10^6\), not \(10^{-3}\). The uppercase \(\text{M}\) and lowercase \(\text{m}\) differ by a factor of \(10^9\), so case cannot be ignored.

question: The unit symbol for a measured length of five metres should be written as
explanation: The SI unit symbol for metre is \(\text{m}\). Unit symbols are not made plural, so the symbol remains \(\text{m}\) even when the value is \(5\). A full stop is not added after a unit symbol unless it ends a sentence for ordinary punctuation. The symbol \(\text{M}\) is not the metre symbol; case matters in SI notation. Writing \(5\,\text{m}\) keeps the numerical value, space, and unit symbol in the standard measurement-record form.

question: A practical notebook records a mass as \(2.0\,\text{kgs}\). The notation should be repaired as
explanation: The SI unit symbol for kilogram is \(\text{kg}\). Unit symbols do not take a plural \(\text{s}\), so \(\text{kgs}\) is not the standard symbol. The letter case is also fixed; \(\text{Kg}\) and \(\text{KG}\) are not the standard SI symbol for kilogram. A full stop is not part of the unit symbol. The repaired record \(2.0\,\text{kg}\) gives the value and unit without changing the measured mass.

question: The notation \(12\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) represents
explanation: The factor \(\text{s}^{-1}\) means division by \(\text{s}\), or “per second.” Therefore \(12\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) means \(12\) metres per second. It is the usual unit form for speed or velocity in SI. The expression is not \(\text{m s}\), which would mean metre multiplied by second. Negative powers in unit notation compactly show division by that unit.

question: The symbol pair \(\text{m}\) and \(\text{M}\) must not be interchanged because
opt_a: \(\text{m}\) and \(\text{M}\) always mean the same unit
opt_c: SI notation treats letter case as meaningful
opt_d: uppercase symbols are always used for base units
explanation: SI symbols are case-sensitive, so changing lowercase to uppercase can change the meaning. The lowercase \(\text{m}\) is the symbol for metre when used as a unit. The uppercase \(\text{M}\) is used as the prefix symbol for mega, meaning \(10^6\), when attached to a unit. For example, \(\text{mW}\) and \(\text{MW}\) represent very different powers. Careful use of case prevents a small writing change from producing a huge numerical error.

question: A force multiplied by displacement may be written as \(20\,\text{N m}\). In this unit record, \(\text{N m}\) means
explanation: A space between unit symbols in a compound unit usually represents multiplication. Thus \(\text{N m}\) means newton multiplied by metre. This is the unit of work or energy and is also called joule, written as \(\text{J}\). Division is shown using a negative power, a slash where allowed, or an equivalent denominator form. The space in \(\text{N m}\) is therefore part of the unit structure, not a plural marker.

question: The record \(8\,\text{m/s}\) is rewritten using negative powers as
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given unit form:} \) \(\text{m/s}\).
\( \textbf{Meaning of slash:} \) The slash means metre divided by second.
\( \textbf{Negative-power rule:} \) Dividing by a unit is written by giving that unit power \(-1\).
So,
\[
\frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}}=\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Apply to the record:} \)
\[
8\,\text{m/s}=8\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
The unit \(\text{m}^{-1}\text{s}\) would mean seconds per metre, the reciprocal kind of unit.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The negative-power form is \(8\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).

question: A measurement label shows \(25\text{kg}\) without spacing. In standard writing, it is better written as
explanation: In a measurement record, a space is normally kept between the numerical value and the unit symbol. Thus \(25\,\text{kg}\) is the preferred form. The symbol \(\text{kg}\) is not pluralised, even when the number is greater than \(1\). A full stop is not part of the unit symbol. The number should come before the unit because the measurement states how many units are being used.

question: A unit line reads: \(1\,\text{W}=1\,\text{J}/\text{s}\). The same relation in compact SI power notation is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Starting relation:} \) \(1\,\text{W}=1\,\text{J}/\text{s}\).
The slash shows division by time.
Using negative powers,
\[
\frac{1}{\text{s}}=\text{s}^{-1}
\]
Therefore,
\[
1\,\text{J}/\text{s}=1\,\text{J s}^{-1}
\]
So,
\[
1\,\text{W}=1\,\text{J s}^{-1}
\]
The option \(1\,\text{J s}\) would mean joule multiplied by second, not joule per second.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(1\,\text{W}=1\,\text{J s}^{-1}\).

question: Scientific notation expresses \(4\,500\,000\,\text{m}\) as
explanation: Scientific notation writes a number as a coefficient between \(1\) and \(10\) multiplied by a power of \(10\). Moving the decimal point in \(4\,500\,000\) to get \(4.5\) requires \(6\) places. Therefore \(4\,500\,000=4.5\times10^6\). The unit \(\text{m}\) remains attached because only the numerical form has changed. A negative power would represent a very small length, not a large one.

question: A small length is written as \(0.000\,032\,\text{m}\). Its scientific notation is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given value:} \) \(0.000\,032\,\text{m}\).
Scientific notation needs a coefficient from \(1\) up to but not including \(10\).
The decimal point is moved \(5\) places to the right to make \(3.2\).
Since the original number is smaller than \(1\), the power of \(10\) must be negative.
Thus,
\[
0.000\,032=3.2\times10^{-5}
\]
The unit \(\text{m}\) is unchanged during the notation change.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(0.000\,032\,\text{m}=3.2\times10^{-5}\,\text{m}\).

question: For a rough scale comparison, \(7.8\times10^3\,\text{kg}\) is closest to the order of magnitude
explanation: Order of magnitude means the nearest power of \(10\) used for a rough scale estimate. The number \(7.8\times10^3\) lies between \(10^3\) and \(10^4\). Since \(7.8\) is closer to \(10\) than to \(1\), the nearest power is \(10^4\). This does not mean the exact value is \(10^4\,\text{kg}\); it only gives the scale of the quantity. Order-of-magnitude thinking helps compare very large or very small measurements quickly.

question: A distance record gives the radius of Earth as approximately \(6.4\times10^6\,\text{m}\). Its order of magnitude is best taken as
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given value:} \) \(6.4\times10^6\,\text{m}\).
For nearest-power order of magnitude, compare the coefficient \(6.4\) with \(1\) and \(10\).
The coefficient \(6.4\) is closer to \(10\) than to \(1\).
So,
\[
6.4\times10^6\approx10\times10^6=10^7
\]
The exact radius is not being replaced by \(10^7\,\text{m}\); the value is only being classified by scale.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The order of magnitude is \(10^7\,\text{m}\).

question: The statement that best describes why scientific notation is useful in measurements is
opt_b: it changes an approximate value into an exact value
opt_c: it makes every physical quantity dimensionless
opt_d: it removes the need for units
explanation: Scientific notation uses powers of \(10\) to write very large or very small numbers in a compact form. For example, \(0.000\,000\,001\,\text{m}\) can be written as \(1\times10^{-9}\,\text{m}\). The unit remains necessary because the power-of-ten form only changes the way the number is written. Scientific notation also makes scale comparison easier because the exponent shows the size range. It does not make an approximate measurement exact.

question: A nucleus has a typical radius of about \(10^{-15}\,\text{m}\), while an atom has a typical radius of about \(10^{-10}\,\text{m}\). The atom is larger by a factor of about
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given scales:} \) Atomic radius \(\approx10^{-10}\,\text{m}\), nuclear radius \(\approx10^{-15}\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Required comparison:} \) Factor by which atom is larger than nucleus.
\( \textbf{Ratio:} \)
\[
\frac{10^{-10}}{10^{-15}}
\]
Use the rule \(\frac{10^a}{10^b}=10^{a-b}\):
\[
\frac{10^{-10}}{10^{-15}}=10^{-10-(-15)}
\]
\[
=10^5
\]
So the atom is about \(10^5\) times larger in radius than the nucleus.
The positive exponent appears because the atom has the larger length scale.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The atom is larger by a factor of about \(10^5\).

question: A time interval of \(3.0\times10^{-9}\,\text{s}\) is compared with \(3.0\times10^{-6}\,\text{s}\). The second interval is
explanation:
\( \textbf{First interval:} \) \(t_1=3.0\times10^{-9}\,\text{s}\).
\( \textbf{Second interval:} \) \(t_2=3.0\times10^{-6}\,\text{s}\).
\( \textbf{Comparison ratio:} \)
\[
\frac{t_2}{t_1}=\frac{3.0\times10^{-6}}{3.0\times10^{-9}}
\]
Cancel the common factor \(3.0\):
\[
\frac{t_2}{t_1}=10^{-6-(-9)}
\]
\[
=10^3
\]
Thus the second interval is \(1000\) times the first.
A less negative exponent represents a larger number when comparing powers of \(10\) below \(1\).
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The second interval is \(10^3\) times the first.

question: A scale list is arranged from smaller to larger length as
explanation: Powers of \(10\) can be compared directly when the same unit is used. Among negative powers, \(10^{-15}\) is smaller than \(10^{-10}\) because it is farther below \(1\). Positive powers are much larger than negative powers, so \(10^3\,\text{m}\) comes after \(10^{-10}\,\text{m}\). Finally, \(10^7\,\text{m}\) is larger than \(10^3\,\text{m}\). The ordering is based on the exponent after confirming that all quantities are expressed in \(\text{m}\).

question: A metre scale is most suitable for measuring
opt_a: the distance between Earth and a star
opt_b: the length of a classroom table
opt_c: the thickness of a single paper sheet with high precision
explanation: A metre scale is suitable for ordinary lengths that can be placed along the scale directly. The length of a classroom table is large enough to be measured with a metre scale or measuring tape. The diameter of an atom is far too small for direct measurement with such an instrument. The thickness of a single paper sheet is usually smaller than the least count of a metre scale, so an indirect or more precise method is needed. Astronomical distances require special indirect methods because they cannot be measured by placing a scale between the two points.

question: The least count of an instrument means
opt_a: the average of all repeated readings
opt_b: the largest value that can be measured by the instrument
opt_d: the number of times the instrument is used
explanation: Least count is the smallest measurement that an instrument can reliably show. For example, if the smallest division on a metre scale is \(1\,\text{mm}\), then its least count is \(1\,\text{mm}\). A smaller least count usually allows finer measurement, though errors may still be present. The largest measurable value is the range of the instrument, not the least count. Least count tells how closely the instrument can resolve nearby values.

question: A ruler has \(10\) equal divisions between \(0\,\text{cm}\) and \(1\,\text{cm}\). Its least count is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given scale information:} \) The distance from \(0\,\text{cm}\) to \(1\,\text{cm}\) is divided into \(10\) equal parts.
\( \textbf{Meaning of least count:} \) The least count is the value of the smallest division on the scale.
\( \textbf{Smallest division value:} \)
\[
\text{least count}=\frac{1\,\text{cm}}{10}
\]
\[
=0.1\,\text{cm}
\]
Since \(1\,\text{cm}=10\,\text{mm}\),
\[
0.1\,\text{cm}=1\,\text{mm}
\]
So the ruler can directly read lengths to \(1\,\text{mm}\).
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The least count is \(0.1\,\text{cm}\).

question: For estimating the thickness of one sheet of paper using an ordinary scale, a better method is to
opt_a: use only the printed page number as the thickness
opt_b: measure a stack and divide by the number of sheets
opt_c: fold the scale and compare it with the sheet
opt_d: measure one sheet directly and ignore the least count
explanation: A single sheet of paper is usually too thin to be measured accurately by an ordinary scale. Measuring many sheets together gives a larger thickness that is easier to read. Dividing the total thickness by the number of sheets gives the average thickness of one sheet. This indirect method reduces the effect of the scale’s least count on the final value. The method assumes that the sheets are nearly identical and are pressed together without large gaps.

question: A stack of \(80\) identical sheets has a total thickness of \(8.0\,\text{mm}\). The thickness of one sheet is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) Number of sheets \(=80\), total thickness \(=8.0\,\text{mm}\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Thickness of one sheet.
\( \textbf{Method:} \) Since one sheet is too thin for a reliable direct scale reading, divide the total thickness by the number of identical sheets.
\[
\text{thickness of one sheet}=\frac{\text{total thickness}}{\text{number of sheets}}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
\text{thickness of one sheet}=\frac{8.0\,\text{mm}}{80}
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
\frac{8.0}{80}=0.10
\]
So the thickness is \(0.10\,\text{mm}\).
Measuring the stack first makes the reading larger and more reliable than trying to read one sheet directly.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The thickness of one sheet is \(0.10\,\text{mm}\).

question: A measuring tape is preferred over a metre scale for measuring the length of a curved boundary because
opt_a: a tape always removes all measurement errors
opt_b: it can follow the curved boundary
opt_c: a metre scale cannot measure any length
opt_d: a tape has no least count
explanation: A flexible measuring tape can be placed along a curved boundary more conveniently than a rigid metre scale. The tape still has a least count, so it does not remove all measurement uncertainty. The metre scale can measure straight lengths well, but it is not ideal for following a curve. Choosing an instrument depends on the shape and size of the length to be measured. A suitable instrument reduces practical difficulty without making the measurement perfect.

question:
